title: The charter
hookLine: the Medina charter makes the city's tribes, including its Jewish tribes, one community for defense

cards: Clan after clan, written down one by one. That's how the document reads. Medina wasn't an empty town waiting for newcomers.

It held Arab clans with old feuds between them, Jewish tribes with their own long histories there, and now emigrants from Mecca, far from home. Any of them could ask: whose city is this now? Who protects whom?
Who pays when someone is hurt? The sirah of Ibn Ishaq preserves a written answer, drawn up under the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Today: the charter.

teach.h: ONE UMMAH, NAMED CLAN BY CLAN.
teach.b: As Ibn Ishaq gives it, the charter opens by naming the believers of Quraysh and of Yathrib, and those who join them and strive alongside them, and declares that they are one community, one ummah.

Then it gets practical, clan by clan: each keeps its old customs for paying blood money and ransoming its captives, fairly and kindly. No one is to leave a debtor stranded. Then it turns to the Jewish tribes of the city.

The Jews of the clan of Awf are named a community alongside the believers: to the Jews their religion, and to the believers theirs. Other Jewish clans are named in the same way. Each side bears its own expenses.

They're to help one another against anyone who attacks the people of the document, and they owe one another sincere advice. And the valley of Yathrib is declared sacred for the people of the document.
What kind of unity is this? It doesn't make everyone the same.
Each clan keeps its customs; each religion keeps its own practice.
It's a one made of many named parts, each listed, none erased.
What binds them is a promise: to defend the city together, and to bring disputes to God and to Muhammad, not to the old feuds.
Some historians ask how the text came together and when, and the city's later story has hard chapters ahead. But the document itself, as preserved, names party after party and gives each a place.

how: Muslims and historians study the charter of Medina (al-sahifah), preserved in Ibn Ishaq's sirah and other early works, and some Muslims point to it today when they speak of living alongside people of other faiths.

o: a royal grant handing Medina to the Prophet
Medina's written pact naming each clan and tribe
a treaty of surrender signed by Mecca's leaders

s: the charter required everyone in Medina to share one religion
it says: to the Jews their religion, and to the believers theirs.

games.q: you're drafting the terms for a city of feuding clans, newcomers and Jewish tribes. what do you write?
o: each keeps its customs and religion; all defend the city together.
each group governs itself and owes the others nothing.
games.why: the charter keeps each clan's customs and each religion, and binds all the parties to defend the city together.

practice: Think of a group you belong to where things are a little unclear or a little unfair: a household, a team, a shared apartment.

In your mind, write it out like the charter, party by party, naming each person, giving each a fair part to carry, and letting each keep what matters to them. If you pray, you can ask Allah for fairness among you.

wordCard.voice: The charter. The agreement of Medina, preserved by Ibn Ishaq, that names the city's believers and its Jewish tribes, clan by clan, as one community for defense, each keeping its own religion. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'community', the word the charter uses for the people it binds together.

carryVoice: Your line: one community of many. A unity that didn't ask anyone to disappear. Day seven hundred seventy-four, done.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the text of the charter of Medina: one ummah; clan customs of blood money and ransom; the Jews of Banu Awf a community with the believers, each with its religion; mutual defense; Yathrib sacred)
Abu Ubayd, Kitab al-Amwal (another early version of the charter)
